title: Gangtok and East Sikkim on a budget
summary: A budget traveller can see Gangtok, Tsomgo Lake, Rumtek and Aritar on about ₹1,800–2,500 a day by sleeping in guesthouses and homestays, eating in local restaurants, using shared jeeps and sharing permit-day vehicles. The single biggest saving is sharing cars on the days when a reserved vehicle is unavoidable.
meta_description: How to travel Gangtok and East Sikkim cheaply: real daily costs, shared jeeps, pooled permit trips, cheap stays, local food and when prices are lowest.

sections.heading: What a budget day really costs
paras: East Sikkim is not the cheapest part of the Himalaya, but it is far from expensive if you travel the way local people do. The things that push costs up are reserved cars, peak-week hotel rates and eating every meal on MG Marg. Avoid those and the region becomes very manageable.

As a rough guide, a budget traveller sharing a room can expect to spend about ₹1,800–2,500 a day in Gangtok, including a guesthouse room, three local meals, local taxis and a share of one sightseeing trip. Days with a permit trip to Tsomgo cost more, and quiet days in Aritar cost less. The table below sets out typical costs from recent seasons. All prices are indicative and rise in peak weeks.

sections.heading: Getting there and around for less
paras: The cheapest way up from the plains is a shared jeep from Siliguri or NJP to Gangtok, which costs about ₹350–450 a seat and takes 4.5–5.5 hours. Jeeps leave from the Sikkim stand next to the Tenzing Norgay Central Bus Terminus on Hill Cart Road in Siliguri and go when all ten seats are full. Mornings are best, because departures thin out after about 2 pm. SNT buses from their own stand in Siliguri are slower but a little cheaper and have more room for bags.

Inside Gangtok, walk as much as you can in the centre and use the small local taxis for longer hops. They run point to point and charge by the trip, typically ₹100–250, so agree the fare first. The Gangtok ropeway is a cheap way to get a view over the town. For Rumtek and Rhenock, shared jeeps leave from the town's taxi stands and cost a fraction of a reserved car.

If you are flying, compare the cost of a shared jeep from Siliguri with a reserved car from Bagdogra. A reserved car costs about ₹4,000–5,500, which is reasonable for four people but steep for one. Solo travellers can take an auto or bus from the airport into Siliguri and pick up a shared jeep there.

sections.heading: Permit days without the big bill
paras: The trip to Tsomgo Lake and Nathu La is where budgets usually break, because tourists must travel in a registered vehicle with a permit. A reserved car costs ₹3,500–5,000 for Tsomgo and Baba Mandir and ₹5,500–7,500 with Nathu La. For a couple, that is a large share of the trip's cost.

The answer is a pooled vehicle. Travel agents along MG Marg sell individual seats in shared vehicles for about ₹700–1,200 for Tsomgo and Baba Mandir and ₹1,200–2,000 including Nathu La, with the permit included. You hand over your ID and photos the afternoon before and are picked up at 7 or 8 am. You will travel with strangers and cannot choose your stops, but the saving is large.

Other ways to save on permit days are to travel with friends and fill a reserved car, to skip Nathu La and do only Tsomgo and Baba Mandir, and to avoid the peak weeks when agents raise fares because cars are short. Do not skip the spare day, though; losing a pre-paid trip to snow costs more than one extra night in a guesthouse.
list: Ask two or three agents for pooled seat prices; they vary.
Check whether the price includes the permit and Baba Mandir.
Hire boots and coats only if you need them; ₹100–200 each.
Pack your own snacks and a flask; food at the lake is pricey.

sections.heading: Where to sleep cheaply
paras: Gangtok has plenty of guesthouses and small hotels in the ₹1,200–2,500 range, concentrated around MG Marg, Tibet Road, Development Area and the lanes near Lal Market. Rooms are usually clean and have hot water, though views and heating vary. Staying central saves more than it seems, because you will walk to dinner instead of paying for a taxi each evening.

Outside Gangtok, homestays are the budget traveller's best friend. In Aritar and Zuluk, ₹1,200–2,200 per person usually includes dinner and breakfast, which removes the cost of eating out. Rumtek village also has a few simple homestays. Book directly where you can, and confirm what meals are included.

Prices jump during the Durga Puja holidays in October, the Christmas and New Year week, and the school holidays in May and June. If your dates are flexible, March, early April, November and early December give good weather at lower prices. In the monsoon, rooms are cheapest but roads are least reliable.

sections.heading: Eating well for little money
paras: Local food in Gangtok is cheap, filling and good. A plate of momos costs ₹80–150, a bowl of thukpa or a thali meal ₹120–250. The best value is in the small restaurants in the lanes leading down from MG Marg towards Lal Market and in the Kanchenjunga shopping complex, where office workers and students eat. The cafés on MG Marg itself charge more for the same dishes, partly for the seats with a view.

Try Sikkimese and Nepali dishes rather than pizzas and pasta, which cost more and are rarely better here. Gundruk soup, phagshapa, sel roti, aloo dum and the many kinds of momo are all cheap. Buy fruit, nuts and churpi from Lal Market for snacks on long drives. Carry a refillable bottle; Sikkim discourages single-use plastic, and filling up at hotels saves money too.

sections.heading: A sample five-day budget plan
paras: Here is how a careful traveller might spend five days in East Sikkim for about ₹11,000–13,000 per person, sharing a room. The plan uses shared transport throughout and one pooled permit trip. It does not include the Silk Route, which needs a reserved car and is cheaper with a group of four or five.
list: Day 1: Shared jeep Siliguri to Gangtok, guesthouse near MG Marg, dinner near Lal Market (about ₹2,000).
Day 2: Walk to Do Drul Chorten and the Institute of Tibetology, ride the ropeway, hand in documents for the permit (about ₹2,000).
Day 3: Pooled vehicle to Tsomgo, Baba Mandir and, if you are Indian, Nathu La (about ₹3,000).
Day 4: Shared jeep to Rumtek and back, afternoon free (about ₹1,800).
Day 5: Shared jeep to Rhenock, local taxi to Aritar, homestay with dinner and breakfast (about ₹2,500), then down to Siliguri next morning.

sections.heading: Where not to cut corners
paras: Some savings are false economies in the mountains. Do not skip warm clothing to save luggage space; buying a jacket in Gangtok in a hurry costs more than bringing one. Do not take the cheapest unregistered driver for mountain roads, especially in snow or on the Silk Route. And do not plan your trip so tightly that a single landslide or snow day forces you to pay for a last-minute reserved car to catch a train.

Travel insurance that covers delays and medical evacuation is worth its modest cost in the Himalaya. So is a spare night. On a budget trip, time is often the thing you can afford to spend, and in East Sikkim a little extra time is what turns a stressful trip into a relaxed one.

faqs.q: How much money do I need per day in Gangtok?
faqs.a: A budget traveller sharing a room can manage on about ₹1,800–2,500 a day, covering a guesthouse, local meals and local taxis. Days with a permit trip cost more, around ₹2,500–3,500 with a pooled seat. A mid-range traveller with a private car and good hotel should budget ₹4,000–6,000 per person a day.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to get to Gangtok from Siliguri?
faqs.a: SNT buses are the cheapest at about ₹250–350, followed by shared jeeps at about ₹350–450 a seat. Both leave from near the Tenzing Norgay Central Bus Terminus in Siliguri. Jeeps are faster and more frequent. Fares are indicative and rise slightly in peak season.

faqs.q: Is a pooled vehicle to Tsomgo safe and reliable?
faqs.a: Yes. Pooled vehicles are the same registered cars and drivers used for private trips, and the permit system applies equally. The drawbacks are fixed timings, less legroom and no choice of stops. Book through a registered agent on or near MG Marg and confirm what the price includes.

faqs.q: When is the cheapest time to visit East Sikkim?
faqs.a: Rooms are cheapest in the monsoon, from late June to early September, but roads are unreliable and views poor. For a balance of good weather and lower prices, try March, early April, November and early December, avoiding the Durga Puja, Christmas and school holiday weeks.

faqs.q: Can I do the Silk Route on a budget?
faqs.a: Yes, but it needs a reserved car, since there is no regular shared transport above Rongli. Join with four or five people to share the car, stay in homestays with meals included, and spend two nights in Zuluk. That brings the cost to about ₹6,000–9,000 per person for a two-night trip from Siliguri.

Gangtok has a handful of backpacker hostels with dorm beds, usually costing ₹500–900 a night, along with many cheap guesthouses. Dorms are popular with solo travellers and a good place to find people to share permit vehicles. Book ahead in peak weeks, when beds fill quickly.

faqs.q: Do I need to tip in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Tipping is not compulsory but is appreciated. For a driver on a full permit day, ₹200–500 is usual; for a homestay host, a few hundred rupees for good service is generous. In restaurants, rounding up or leaving 5–10 percent is fine. Tips are a good way to reward honest service.

faqs.q: Are ATMs easy to find in East Sikkim?
faqs.a: Gangtok has plenty of ATMs and most shops accept digital payments. Rhenock and Rongli have a few ATMs, but Aritar village and Zuluk have none, and mobile signal is patchy there. Draw enough cash in Gangtok or Siliguri before heading to the Silk Route and homestays.

faqs.q: What is the biggest mistake budget travellers make in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Planning too tightly. One snow day or landslide can cancel a permit trip or delay the drive down, and a missed train costs far more than an extra night. Build in a spare day, especially if Tsomgo or Nathu La is the main reason for your visit.
